clinicalPearls: Dry socket is a painful complication of tooth extraction caused by disintegration or loss of the protective blood clot, exposing alveolar bone
Severe throbbing pain characteristically begins two to four days after extraction, later than the pain of the surgery itself
The socket appears empty with exposed bone and often malodour, but there is usually no purulent discharge or significant systemic upset
It is most common after mandibular molar extractions, particularly lower third molars
Recognised risk factors include smoking, oral contraceptive use, traumatic or difficult extractions, and poor oral hygiene
It is primarily an inflammatory and fibrinolytic process rather than a true infection, so antibiotics are usually not indicated
Management is supportive: irrigation, gentle debridement, and placement of a sedative dressing to relieve pain and protect the bone
Preventive measures include atraumatic technique, avoiding smoking, and good postoperative care
reference.pathophysiology: Dry socket, or alveolar osteitis, develops when the blood clot that normally fills and protects an extraction socket is lost prematurely, often through excessive local fibrinolysis. Breakdown of the clot exposes the alveolar bone and nerve endings to the oral environment, producing intense pain. Contributing factors such as smoking, bacterial contamination, trauma during extraction, and elevated fibrinolytic activity impair clot stability and delay the normal organisation and healing of the socket. The condition is characterised by inflammation of the exposed bone rather than an established suppurative infection.
additionalDifferentials: Retained root fragment or foreign body
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the socket for an absent clot and exposed bone
Assessment for systemic signs to distinguish from spreading infection
Radiography if a retained root, foreign body, or bony pathology is suspected
Review of risk factors including smoking and medication history
Consideration of osteonecrosis risk in patients on antiresorptive therapy
redFlags: Spreading swelling, fever, trismus, or purulent discharge suggesting true infection rather than simple dry socket
Failure to heal or exposed necrotic bone in a patient on antiresorptive or antiangiogenic drugs raising concern for osteonecrosis
Persistent numbness or worsening pain suggesting nerve injury or osteomyelitis
reference.prognosis: Dry socket is self-limiting and typically resolves over one to two weeks with supportive care and adequate analgesia, without long-term sequelae in most patients.
pitfalls: Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated dry socket, which is not an infection
Mistaking spreading infection or osteomyelitis for simple alveolar osteitis
Overlooking a retained root fragment as the cause of persistent socket pain
Failing to consider medication-related osteonecrosis in at-risk patients with non-healing sockets
management: Gently irrigate the socket with warm saline to remove food debris and necrotic material from the exposed bone
Place a sedative obtundent intra-alveolar dressing (for example one containing eugenol) to cover exposed bone and relieve pain, changing it at review as needed
Provide adequate analgesia with simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for the self-limiting inflammatory pain
Avoid routine antibiotics, since this is a fibrinolytic and inflammatory process rather than an established infection
Advise smoking cessation and meticulous oral hygiene with warm saline or antiseptic rinses to support healing
Review until symptoms settle, and image to exclude a retained root, foreign body or bony pathology if pain persists
Escalate and reconsider the diagnosis if spreading infection develops or if the patient is on antiresorptive therapy raising osteonecrosis risk
